Chilean Blockade on Construction Materials Plants Lifted After Government Accord

A week-long blockade of major cement and aggregate production sites in Chile’s Atacama region has ended following intensive negotiations between the government and local authorities. The action, which began on May 29, targeted facilities operated by key players including Cementos del Pacifico and Andes Materials Group, halting output and disrupting the supply of core construction materials nationwide.

The blockade, organized by regional officials in response to a geopolitical dispute over resource allocation, led to the temporary closure of five plants and several distribution depots. According to the Chilean Construction Materials Association (ACMAC), the stoppage affected more than 40% of the country’s cement and aggregate supply, forcing contractors to suspend projects and sparking concerns over delivery timelines.

"With the Atacama facilities offline, we saw immediate shortages in critical materials," said ACMAC president Rodrigo Silva. "Some construction sites in Santiago and Valparaíso were forced to reduce shifts or halt work altogether."

The government announced Monday that a resolution had been reached, restoring access to the plants and allowing full operations to resume. In a joint statement, the Ministry of Mining and the Atacama Regional Council said the agreement included commitments on regional employment and increased investment in local infrastructure.

"The swift resolution demonstrates the importance of dialogue," said Mining Minister María Fernández. "We have ensured the continued operation of an industry vital to Chile’s economic development."

Operations at the affected sites reportedly restarted late Monday, with trucks carrying cement and aggregates dispatched by Tuesday morning. ACMAC estimates that the week-long disruption resulted in production losses of approximately 75,000 tons of cement and 120,000 tons of aggregates.

Industry analysts suggest it could take up to two weeks for supply chains to fully normalize. "Backlogs will persist in the short term, but with operations back on track, most projects should recover by late June," said construction analyst Diego Orellana.

Union representatives welcomed the accord, emphasizing the need for long-term solutions to prevent future disruptions.
